kp.k: Acquisitions mark the early legal AI generation's consolidation
kp.d: Tromans interprets Evisort's agreement to sell to Workday as emblematic of consolidation among legal AI pioneers that gained broader market attention around 2015/2016. His evidence is a selected company history, rather than a comprehensive market study: RAVN sold to iManage in 2017, eBrevia to Donnelly Financial in 2018, Kira Systems to Litera in 2021, Seal Software to DocuSign in 2020 for reportedly $188m cash, and Leverton to MRI in 2019. Workday's Evisort acquisition was announced, not described as completed.
qs: For this site at least, ‘legal AI’ as a subject really got going in the 2010s, coming to broader market attention in around 2015/2016 as a growing number of startups arrived, using machine learning and earlier versions of Natural Language Processing.
Then one-by-one, some quite rapidly, others only just recently, were bought.
Workday announced it will buy the company

kp.k: Consolidation spans research, contract analysis and adjacent software markets
kp.d: The acquisition examples encompass legal research and contract analysis, with buyers including legal information businesses, software companies and a law company. LexisNexis bought LexMachina in 2015 and Ravel in 2017; Elevate acquired LexPredict in 2018; Wolters Kluwer acquired Della AI in 2022; and Sirion acquired Eigen Technologies in 2024. Tromans describes Della and Eigen as second-wave companies and notes Eigen's contract AI was not exclusively legal. These examples concern vendor-market restructuring, not evidence of law-firm staffing changes.
qs: Ravel was sold to LexisNexis not that long after getting noticed in 2017.
– a small, but forward-thinking contract analysis startup created by Dan Katz, sold to Elevate, the law company, in 2018.
– also part of this second wave, also focused on contract AI, but not just for legal. Had Goldman Sachs as an investor. Sold to CLM company Sirion this year (2024).

kp.k: Casetext bridged earlier AI and generative AI
kp.d: Tromans reports that Thomson Reuters bought Casetext for $650m in 2023. He distinguishes its early adoption of large language models from many other pioneers: although founded around ML/NLP, Casetext had already worked extensively with generative AI by ChatGPT's arrival. More generally, the companies surveyed originated with pre-generative machine learning, even when they later adopted generative AI.
qs: – another pioneer in the legal research field, sold to Thomson Reuters for $650m in 2023.
Started very much in the field of ML/NLP, but unlike many others was quick to see the future value in LLMs, and by the time ChatGPT arrived had done plenty of work with genAI.
Some later tapped genAI as well, but that was not the tech they were founded upon.

kp.k: Demand constraints and disputes also interrupted early pioneers
kp.d: Not all early companies exited through acquisition. Tromans attributes RFRNZ's 2021 closure to insufficient demand from German lawyers. He reports that ROSS Intelligence encountered a dispute involving Thomson Reuters in 2020, remained in a minimal form while the dispute continued, and apparently no longer operated as before. Nevertheless, he credits ROSS with raising lawyers' awareness of AI's potential; that is his qualitative assessment, not a measured adoption finding.
qs: – also a German legal AI company, started early, but closed down in 2021 after a lack of demand from lawyers there.
However, ROSS really captured the imagination of many lawyers and did a lot of work to raise the awareness of what legal AI could do.
the company still exists in a very minimal form while its dispute drags on, although doesn’t appear to be operating as it did before.

kp.k: Founders and independent businesses continue beyond acquisition
kp.d: The article qualifies its end-of-an-era framing by describing continuing entrepreneurship and surviving businesses. eBrevia relaunched independently; co-founder Ned Gannon created Coheso for in-house needs; Zuva emerged from Kira's sale; and former Seal team member Jim Wagner created The Contract Network. Tromans also names Noah Waisberg among founders building new legal AI companies. ThoughtRiver continued operating after Tim Pullan stepped away from its top role. Thus, the claimed end concerns an original company cohort, not the disappearance of its founders or all independent pioneers.
qs: And it’s interesting to see just how many of these early founders have gone on to create new legal AI companies, e.g. Ned Gannon, Noah Waisberg and Jim Wagner.
So, while one company they helped to build was sold, that is not the end of their startup journeys.
Although the company is very much still going.

kp.k: External investment is presented as a driver of exits
kp.d: Tromans argues that founders' ambitions differ, from rapid sale to lifelong company building, but external investment means most startups ultimately sell or stop trading after several years. He asserts that very few survive beyond 10 years and that even seven years is doing well. This is an explanatory generalisation offered without a supporting dataset or survival analysis in the document.
qs: Some founders create companies with the sole intention of selling as fast as possible.
Others see their startup as the beginning of a life-long journey and hope to build something massive.
In reality, because of external investment, most startups end up selling (or stop trading) after several years, with very few making it past 10 years, in fact even seven years is doing well.

kp.k: Earlier pioneers legitimised software performing lawyers' work
kp.d: Tromans's central account of professional change is that earlier legal AI companies familiarised buyers with software as a means of performing legal work, rather than merely storing information or providing basic utilities. He characterises current generative AI businesses as a third wave built on different technology but benefiting from that earlier market groundwork. Changing the means of legal production remains, in his view, the shared goal; the article does not quantify resulting productivity or employment effects.
qs: that first wave of legal AI companies helped to make the market familiar with the concept of using software not just as a basic utility or an information storage system, but to actually perform the work of a lawyer:
to change the means of legal production
And that remains the central goal.

kp.k: Generative AI pioneers may repeat the consolidation cycle
kp.d: Looking a few years ahead from 2024, Tromans predicts that the generative legal AI cohort will probably follow a similar trajectory: acquisitions by non-legal conglomerates or the 'Big Two', business failures, and perhaps one or two large independent segment leaders. He cites Harvey, Leya and Robin AI as examples of the expanding new generation, but does not predict individual outcomes for them. The projected cycle is explicitly conditional on history repeating, rather than an established finding.
qs: Also, if history repeats itself – and that seems likely – in a few years from now Artificial Lawyer will be writing an article about where all the legal genAI pioneers went.
X company got bought by a non-legal sector conglomerate. Y and Z companies were bought by one of the Big Two. A and B went bust, or ceased to trade.
And perhaps one or two will just keep going and become huge companies that dominate their market segments.
Now consider the growing number of new ones, from Harvey to Leya to Robin AI, and many more.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Richard Tromans describes consolidation as the end of the first legal-AI pioneer wave and predicts a similar cycle for generative-AI vendors.
pts.d: Tromans argues that most of the early ML/NLP legal-AI pioneers have been acquired or ceased operating independently. He anticipates that many generative-AI startups will likewise be acquired by larger legal or non-legal businesses or cease trading, while perhaps a few will become dominant independent companies. This is a prediction based on the earlier market cycle, not a reported outcome for the new generation. He also stresses continuity: founders of acquired businesses have started new legal-AI ventures, and some early businesses remain independent.

pts.k: Tromans claims early legal-AI businesses prepared the market for software that performs lawyers’ work, laying the groundwork for a generative-AI third wave.
pts.d: The claimed change is from software as a utility or information repository to software performing legal work. Tromans presents changing legal production as the continuing goal of successive AI generations, rather than claiming that lawyers have already been fully replaced. He distinguishes the earlier businesses’ founding ML/NLP technology from generative AI, while acknowledging that some later adopted generative AI.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of named acquisition, closure and founder-reentry examples; the future consolidation claim rests on historical analogy.
pts.d: Tromans lists transactions involving RAVN, eBrevia, Kira Systems, Seal Software, Leverton, Ravel, LexMachina, LexPredict, Della AI, Eigen Technologies and Casetext, alongside Workday’s announced purchase of Evisort. He reports RFRNZ’s closure after insufficient lawyer demand and describes ROSS’s curtailed operations amid its dispute with Thomson Reuters. Examples of continued entrepreneurship include Ned Gannon, Noah Waisberg and Jim Wagner. These are illustrative market histories, not a quantified market-wide dataset. No benchmarks or measured effects on legal productivity, employment or client outcomes are supplied. The proposition that pioneers familiarised the market with AI is Tromans’s interpretation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The retrospective runs from the 2010s to 2024; the forecast is conditional on history repeating over the next few years.
pts.d: Writing in 2024, Tromans dates broader market attention to around 2015–2016 and traces acquisitions through Workday’s then-announced Evisort deal. He predicts a comparable generative-AI consolidation cycle in a few years, without a precise deadline. He links startup exits generally to external investment and says few startups remain beyond seven to ten years, but supplies no survival-rate dataset. Qualifications include independent survivors, eBrevia’s return to independence, ThoughtRiver’s continued operation despite its CEO stepping away, and the possibility that some new vendors become large independent businesses.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The primary affected groups are legal-AI vendors and founders, acquiring businesses, and lawyers using contract-analysis and research tools.
pts.d: The market-structure claims primarily concern technology vendors, their investors and founders, and acquirers such as legal-information companies, software platforms and non-legal conglomerates. The legal-work applications include contract analysis, contract risk assessment, contract lifecycle management and case-law research, serving lawyers and corporate in-house teams. Harvey, Leya and Robin AI are named as members of the growing new generation, not as companies with individually predicted exit outcomes. Elevate is identified as the law company acquiring LexPredict, distinct from software-vendor acquirers. The article does not specify effects on lawyer headcount, fees, staffing structures or access to justice.
